A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AffPCL research and contain readable main texts and Appendices A–G. Equations, algorithms, references, and retained figures can be matched across the revision, supporting a reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic multi-agent simulations, including baseline comparisons, heterogeneity sweeps, and agent-specific results in Figures 1–4 and Appendix B.

after.justification: V2 reports original synthetic, FEMNIST, and SARSA experiments in Figures 1–6 and Appendix B, including a comparison involving estimated density ratios.

M1.justification: The core AffPCL updates and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. V2 adds limited task-specific adaptations: the FEMNIST implementation omits importance correction, while the SARSA implementation uses evolving softmax policies and a density-ratio estimator based on state visitation frequencies.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates synthetic linear systems only. V2 additionally evaluates personalized digit/curved-letter regression on FEMNIST and SARSA control with heterogeneous rewards and transition kernels. V1 already discussed reinforcement learning theoretically in Appendix C.6, but did not report these experiments.

E2.justification: The synthetic comparison expands from independent learning and FedAvg to also include fine-tuning, pFedMe, Ditto, and clustered FL, all appearing in v2 Figure 1. These additions substantially broaden the comparison to personalized-learning alternatives.

E3.justification: V2 adds distinct FEMNIST and SARSA protocols, including test-label MSE and MSE against optimal Q-functions obtained by value iteration, with new feature dimensions, budgets, and controls. Section 7 also changes the synthetic medium/high heterogeneity levels from 0.2/0.5 to 0.3/0.8, although Appendix B retains the earlier values, leaving those settings inconsistent.

E4.justification: V2 Figure 3 adds a targeted comparison of AffPCL with and without estimated density ratios across heterogeneity levels, testing whether asynchronous estimation harms learning. The earlier heterogeneity heatmaps, agent-count contours, and agent-specific analysis remain unchanged as Figures 4–6.

E5.justification: Both versions specify 10 runs and 90% confidence regions in Appendix B. V2 retains shaded uncertainty displays without documenting a changed repetition count, confidence level, seed protocol, or statistical testing procedure.

E6.justification: Figure 1 contains revised curves and results for four additional baselines. New Figures 2–3 report FEMNIST test MSE and SARSA Q-function MSE, including similar performance with and without estimated density ratios. The synthetic medium/high cases cannot support direct same-setting improvement claims because their reported settings differ and are inconsistent within v2.

T1.justification: New Remark 1 in Appendix C.1 adds mathematical communication and computation cost accounting relative to FedAvg, reporting up to fourfold communication and sixfold per-agent computation overhead. The convergence theorems, density-ratio lower bound, assumptions, and existing proofs remain unchanged; no nonlinear SARSA convergence proof is added.

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions, and central conclusion retain the same claims about full personalization, adaptive affinity-based speedup, independent-learning-level worst-case rates, and agent-specific gains. Additional experiments and expanded future directions do not redefine these core contributions.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly discusses the communication/computation overhead accompanying personalization and possible ways to reduce it in Appendix C.1. Figure 3 also introduces the interpretation that density estimation is relatively inexpensive compared with policy optimization, based on the similar learning curves with and without estimated ratios.

D1.justification: Appendix B substantially expands implementation information: fine-tuning uses 30 federated plus 30 local steps, pFedMe and Ditto use regularization 15, and clustered FL uses 10 clusters. It also documents FEMNIST feature and label construction, batching and communication settings, and SARSA hyperparameters, reference computation, and density estimation.

R1.justification: V2 adds Zhang, Chen, and Di (2025) to the density-ratio discussion. The principal related-work positioning remains unchanged. Numerous other author, year, and venue edits, including FedBR and FedDC, refer to works already cited in v1.

P1.justification: The progressive method exposition and section organization remain intact. Local revisions organize Section 7 into synthetic, real-world, and reinforcement-learning paragraphs, enumerate baselines in Appendix B, and add the cost discussion. Author affiliation, publication headers, and bibliography presentation are also edited.

P2.justification: The empirical presentation substantially expands: Figure 1 is rebuilt with additional comparator curves and a larger legend, and two new four-panel figures present FEMNIST and SARSA results on a consolidated results page. Earlier appendix Figures 2–4 are retained as Figures 4–6, rather than replaced.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens empirical support that v1 limited to synthetic systems and two basic baselines. Personalized FL comparators, FEMNIST, SARSA, and the density-estimation comparison address important gaps in comparative and practical validation; the cost analysis adds transparency. These gains outweigh the reporting weaknesses, although conflicting synthetic heterogeneity settings and omitted FEMNIST importance correction limit reproducibility and how directly the new experiments validate the complete method.
